transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jason Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Luca Chen (Redwood SRE), Maria Alvarez (Acme CTO), Rahul Patel (Acme Platform Eng), Sonia Green (Acme ML Eng), Tom (Acme infra)

Summary (auto-gen, may be noisy): Quick technical deep dive on throughput tuning for Acme's long-context robotic planning workload. Focus areas: continuous batching behavior, scheduler kno bs/knobs (sic), max_num_seqs tuning, token limits, KV-cache effects, quantization impact on throughput, and on-prem/VPC deployment constraints. Action items and benchmark plan agreed.

[00:00] Jason: Alright, thanks everyone for joining. Quick roll call, and then Priya will walk through the tuning primitives we usually use.
[00:12] Maria: Hi, yes hi, Maria here. We have Sonia, Rahul and Tom on. Thanks for doing this. We're trying to push throughput on our planning inference - long sequences, variable length, lots of prefix reuse, so curious where to start.
[00:25] Priya: Hey everyone. Just to flag, I'll cover continuous batching and scheduler knobs, then Luca will cover infra considerations for VPC and on-prem, and we'll close with a proposed benchmark. Sound good?
[00:35] Rahul: Yup. Important, we run 8-16 simultaneous sequences per request sometimes, and token length spikes up to 12-16K tokens during belief-state dumps. We need predictable tail latency and high sustained throughput.
[00:49] Priya: Great, that context helps. Ok, so continuous batching - high level: instead of fixed micro-batches, the runtime accepts live requests into a batch up to scheduling windows and resource caps. We tune the scheduling window and max_num_seqs to balance latency vs utilization.
[01:12] [01:13] Speaker 1: (mumble) is that the same as dynamic batching?
[01:16] Priya: Sort of, yes. Dynamic vs continuous semantics differ in our runtime: continuous batching is lower-level, it keeps an open pipeline, maintains KV cache warmness between steps, and core scheduling knobs are: scheduling_window_ms, max_batch_tokens, max_num_seqs, and pack_short_seqs.
[01:33] Sonia: When you say "pack_short_seqs" does that mess with prefix alignment? Our prompts often start with a common 1k token header then diverge.
[01:42] Priya: Good question. Pack_short_seqs will pack multiple short sequences into a physical batch to increase utilization. If you have long common prefixes, that's actually beneficial for KV cache hits because identical prefixes produce identical KV keys and we avoid re-computing. But be careful with padding overhead if sequences are disparate.
[02:02] [02:04] Jason: Also note quantization interacts — 8-bit quantized kernels have different throughput curves for long tokens; sometimes quantization increases per-token latency but reduces memory pressure enabling larger batch sizes.
[02:18] Rahul: We've seen weird thrashing where throughput drops when too many long sequences are in-flight. We suspect KV cache eviction and memory GC. Any guidance?
[02:29] Luca: Yeah, thrashing often indicates the runtime is hitting token or KV capacity limits. We expose max_cache_tokens_per_gpu and cache_eviction_policy. For sustained long-contexts you want to increase max_cache_tokens_per_gpu, set eviction policy to least-recently-used with a high watermark, and align your max_num_seqs so the batch isn't over-subscribed.
[02:49] Sonia: Can we increase kv cache without blowing memory on a 48GB GPU?
[02:53] Priya: You can, but you must tradeoff model size or quantization. Common pattern: switch to 4-bit or mixed-int8/4 quant profile for the model weights to free ~20-30% memory, then raise cache tokens. We have a quant profile called q4_0 and q8_mixed in our catalog. q4 tends to be faster for large batch throughput on Ampere/Hopper-like GPUs, but for single-request latency it sometimes regresses.
[03:18] [03:19] Tom: Our on-prem GPUs are older A100 40G, so memory is tighter. Is there a recommended scheduler configuration for fewer-memory devices?
[03:28] Priya: Yes - for 40G, reduce max_num_seqs, lower max_batch_tokens, and use aggressive packing of short seqs but cap pack size to avoid padding blowup. Also tune scheduling_window_ms small (20-40ms) to reduce tail latency if you can't batch large.
[03:44] Maria: We're sensitive to tail p99 latency; our SLA is 300ms p99 for interactive planning callbacks. Can you still use continuous batching?
[03:53] Priya: You can; you just need to calibrate the scheduling_window_ms and prioritization. We have a hybrid policy: low-latency queue (priority) with a tiny scheduling window, and background high-util queue which uses larger windows and bigger max_num_seqs. Requests tagged as interactive go to the low-latency queue. That keeps p99 tight while allowing batch throughput for background jobs.
[04:17] [04:18] Rahul: How do you tag requests? We use headers in our client SDK.
[04:21] Jason: Yep, client SDK supports route-level tags, priority headers, and token budgets. You can set route.max_tokens_per_request, route.priority: interactive or batch, etc.
[04:32] Sonia: Back to KV cache — what about partial prefix sharing? Some sequences share the first 2k tokens only. Does the runtime deduplicate per-token or per-key?
[04:40] Priya: Dedup is at KV key granularity which is derived from past positions and attention context; practically, shared prefixes yield cache hits for those positions. However, if you have different masking or special tokens appended, that reduces hit rate. We recommend normalizing prefixes and using a canonicalization step when possible.
[04:59] [05:02] Speaker 2: (background noise)
[05:05] Luca: Another practical knob is max_num_seqs versus max_batch_tokens. If you set max_num_seqs high but max_batch_tokens low, you'll get many small batches and overhead increases. Conversely, high max_batch_tokens with low max_num_seqs can let a few huge sequences dominate. We suggest profiling with a matrix: max_num_seqs = [8,16,32], max_batch_tokens = [8k,16k,32k] for your workload.
[05:33] Sonia: Ok, do you have metrics we'd expect? Like tokens/sec and p50/p99 ranges per config?
[05:39] Priya: We do. For example on a 4xA100-80G dedicated pool with q4_0 and kv_cache tuned, continuous batching with max_num_seqs=32 and max_batch_tokens=32k achieved ~220k tokens/sec with p50 ≈ 45ms and p99 ≈ 300-350ms for mixed 2-16K seqs. But on 40G and q8_mixed you'd see ~80-120k tokens/sec and higher p99. These are illustrative; we'll run your exact model to give you numbers.
[06:10] [06:11] Rahul: What about scheduler fairness? If one tenant issues many short prompts and another uses long sequences, do you isolate?
[06:18] Priya: We have per-tenant rate caps and soft isolation via route weights. On Dedicated, you can pin GPUs to tenants. Our scheduler supports weighted-fair queuing across priorities so short prompt tenants don't starve long-run jobs if configured. There's also an autoscale/burst policy to reserve capacity for high-priority requests.
[06:39] Maria: On VPC/on-prem side, what are the main gotchas?
[06:43] Luca: Network egress and firewall rules are common. Also, kernel compatibility for quantized ops — some environments need specific CUDA/MPS and cuBLAS versions; our on-prem package includes a compatibility matrix. For KV cache persistence across restarts you need a shared NVMe or host-managed mem-mapped file; we expose an option to checkpoint KV shards every N minutes.
[07:08] Sonia: If we checkpoint KV, does it rehydrate quickly? That is, can we warm the cache and avoid cold-start penalties?
[07:14] Priya: Yes, but warm-up time depends on size; incremental rehydration streaming works well. A recommended pattern: when service restarts, load last N prefixes that match your high-frequency prefixes; we provide a CLI to import a prefix set.
[07:29] [07:31] Jason: Quick aside: token limits — if you plan for 16K tokens, confirm that the model architecture and attention kernel support that sequence length efficiently. Some older custom models degrade quadratically.
[07:44] Rahul: We're using a 70B transformer variant with patched rotary embeddings up to 20K. Any special handling?
[07:50] Priya: Rotary scaled embeddings are fine. Watch for kv index size; the model kv per token footprint times 20K tokens can be large. Consider using compressed KV storage (we offer a 2:1 compression option for cold segments). Also, if you do chunked generation with incremental returns you can reduce memory by streaming partial outputs and releasing prefixes when no longer needed.
[08:14] [08:16] Speaker 3: (laugh)
[08:18] Sonia: About quantization — you said q4_0 might regress single-request latency. Why would that be?
[08:24] Priya: Quantization changes kernel characteristics. Int4 kernels sometimes have lower single-thread throughput due to indexing overhead; but they reduce memory allowing more parallelism. For throughput-heavy workloads that benefit from larger batch sizes, quant helps. For ultra-low-latency single-shot, int8 or fp16 might be better. We recommend experimenting with two profiles in staging.
[08:45] Maria: Can Redwood run both profiles and auto-fallback based on request type?
[08:49] Jason: Yes, model variants and rollout policies let you route interactive to the low-latency variant and batch to quantized high-throughput variant. Automatic fallback can go to a compatible variant if capacity issues happen.
[09:02] [09:03] Rahul: Memory GC earlier — is that managed in process or by the runtime? We saw OOMs and orphaned GPU memory after canceled requests.
[09:12] Luca: We have a reclamation thread that sweeps caches and frees KV segments marked for eviction. OOMs on canceled requests usually point to pinned tensors not released because of a stuck accelerator context; we added heuristics to force a GC on cancellation and to limit pinned buffer counts. We'll need logs to diagnose.
[09:31] Sonia: We'll send a few recent crash dumps.
[09:34] Priya: For the benchmark we propose: 2-hour continuous run, simulated arrival distribution matching your 9-17 UTC peak, varied priority mix (70% interactive, 30% batch), sequence length distribution you provide. We'll iterate on the scheduling matrix and provide a recommended config file for your private cluster.
[09:55] [09:56] Jason: Ok let's open it to a short Q&A before closing.
[09:59] Maria: One last question — for p99 guarantees, do you folks recommend Dedicated or Private? We want both low-latency and data control.
[10:08] Priya: Dedicated is often sufficient — you get reserved GPU pools and SLA-backed latency. Private gives you more control over network and can lower jitter if you colocate; but it increases ops overhead. For regulatory/data residency reasons Private may be necessary; from a pure latency standpoint, Dedicated in the same cloud region with pinned resources is easier to manage.
[10:31] Rahul: Any quick tips for initial config to avoid immediate overload?
[10:35] Priya: Start conservative: scheduling_window_ms = 30, max_num_seqs = 8, max_batch_tokens = 8k, enable pack_short_seqs, set kv_max_tokens_per_gpu = 25000 for 80G-class GPUs (scale down for 40G). Ramp up by factor 2 in steps.
[10:54] [10:55] Jason: Great — we'll circulate the playbook and the matrix. Thanks everyone.
[10:59] Maria: Thanks, super helpful. We'll get those traces over.
[11:04] End notes: brief mention of documents shared: link to "redwood-throughput-playbook-v2.pdf" (sent after call), share quant profile comparison sheet, and a small demo notebook.
